Notebook vs script vs interpreter?
column2: Notebook: cells run in the order you execute them (restart and run all before trusting it). Script: runs top to bottom every time; used for production and verify scripts. Interpreter: one line at a time, for quick checks.

column1: What is a virtual environment for?
column2: A per-project interpreter and package set (python -m venv .venv; pip install -r requirements.txt), so versions can be pinned and one project's upgrade cannot break another.
3.5, 3, -4, 1. / always gives a float; // rounds toward minus infinity; % takes the divisor's sign so a == (a // b) * b + a % b. (C truncates: -7 / 2 is -3.)
0.1, 0.2 and 0.3 are each rounded to binary64; the rounded sum is one step (5.55e-17) above float(0.3). Compare with math.isclose or a tolerance, never ==.

column1: float64 facts to know?
column2: 53 significant bits (~15–17 digits), machine epsilon 2^-52 ≈ 2.22e-16, largest ≈ 1.8e308, integers exact up to 2^53 ≈ 9.0e15. Python int has unlimited size.

column1: List, tuple, dict, set?
column2: list: ordered, mutable. tuple: ordered, immutable. dict: key → value, fast look-up. set: unique items, fast membership. Index from 0; s[a:b] has b − a items.

column1: b = a for a list: what happens?
column2: No copy: b is a second name for the same list, so a change through either name shows in both. Copy with list(a) (shallow) or copy.deepcopy(a). 'is' tests identity, '==' tests value.

column1: Why is [[0] * 3] * 3 a bug?
column2: It holds three references to one inner list, so setting grid[0][0] changes every row. Use [[0] * 3 for _ in range(3)].

column1: The mutable-default trap?
column2: def f(x, acc=[]) evaluates [] once, at definition, so calls share it. Use acc=None and create the list inside.

column1: Comprehension syntax?
column2: [expr for x in items if condition]; also {k: v for ...} and {x for ...}. Use for simple transforms; use a loop when logic needs more than a line.

column1: How should a function handle invalid input?
column2: Raise a specific exception (raise ValueError('…')) with a clear message, rather than return a plausible wrong value. Callers catch specific exceptions; never use a bare except:.

column1: How to read a traceback?
column2: From the bottom up: last line = exception type and message; above it, the failing line; above that, the chain of calls that led there.

column1: Reading numbers from a CSV safely?
column2: Use the csv module (csv.DictReader), open files in a with block, and convert fields with float/int: text '1000' sorts before '993'.

column1: Bisection in one line?
column2: Keep an interval where f changes sign and halve it until it is shorter than tol: ceil(log2(width/tol)) steps (34 to go from 1 to 1e-10). Needs only f's values.

column1: Why is NumPy faster than a Python loop?
column2: Arrays store raw values contiguously with one dtype, and each operation is one call into compiled code; a list holds references to objects and a loop pays interpreter overhead per element. Typical gain 10–100×.

column1: linspace vs arange?
column2: np.linspace(a, b, n): n points including both ends (use for floats). np.arange(start, stop, step): stop excluded; float steps can add or drop an end point by rounding.

column1: Broadcasting rules?
column2: Compare shapes from the last axis back: sizes must be equal or 1; size 1 stretches; missing leading axes count as 1. (12,1) with (1,12) → (12,12); (3,4) with (3,) → error.

column1: Slice vs mask selection: view or copy?
column2: Basic slices (x[::2], x[1:4]) are views sharing memory; boolean masks and index arrays return copies. Check with np.shares_memory; use .copy() before modifying a selection you need to keep.

column1: Combining conditions on arrays?
column2: Use & | ~ with parentheses, e.g. (v > 0.97) & (v < 1.03); 'and'/'or' raise an error for arrays. mask.sum() counts, mask.mean() gives the fraction.

column1: uint8 200 + 100 in NumPy?
column2: 44: fixed-width integers wrap modulo 2^8. Under NumPy 2 (NEP 50) a Python int adapts to the array's dtype, so the result stays uint8. Widen first with astype(np.int16).

column1: float16, float32, float64 precision?
column2: Significand 11 / 24 / 53 bits; ε ≈ 9.8e-4 / 1.2e-7 / 2.2e-16; max 65504 / 3.4e38 / 1.8e308. float32 integers exact only to 2^24 ≈ 1.7e7. bfloat16: float32's 8-bit exponent, 7 fraction bits.

column1: IEEE 754 binary64 layout?
column2: Sign bit, 11-bit exponent (bias 1023), 52-bit fraction: x = (−1)^s × 1.f × 2^(e−1023). The implicit leading 1 gives 53 significant bits.

column1: NaN behavior?
column2: Produced by 0/0, inf − inf; propagates through arithmetic; nan == nan is False. Detect with np.isnan; np.nanmean etc. skip it deliberately.

column1: Catastrophic cancellation and its cure?
column2: Subtracting nearly equal numbers leaves mostly rounding error: (1 − cos 1e-8)/1e-16 gives 0, not 0.5. Rewrite algebraically: 1 − cos x = 2 sin²(x/2). Also: two-pass variance, stable quadratic roots c/(a·x_large).

column1: Why does np.sum beat a running sum?
column2: It adds pairwise (a tree), so error grows ~ε·log2 n instead of ~ε·n. A float32 running sum of a million 0.1s gives 100958; np.sum 100000.01; accumulate float32 data in float64.

column1: RMS and crest factor of common waves?
column2: Sine: RMS = A/√2, crest √2. Triangle: A/√3, crest √3. Square: A, crest 1. Crest factor = peak/RMS sets headroom.

column1: Reproducible random numbers?
column2: rng = np.random.default_rng(seed): same seed, same stream on every machine. Seed every reported simulation and test; vary seeds to check robustness.

column1: Quick least-squares line?
column2: gain, offset = np.polyfit(x, y, 1); check residuals y − (gain·x + offset) for trends (nonlinearity) versus scatter (noise).

column1: Bracketing versus guess-based root-finders?
column2: Bracketing (bisection, brentq) needs an interval where f changes sign and always converges inside it. Guess-based (newton/secant) is faster near the root but can wander, run out of iterations or stop at a non-root.

column1: Why check a root by substituting it back?
column2: SciPy's secant-based newton stops when successive estimates agree, not when f ≈ 0; from a bad guess it can return a point with a residual of milliamperes. f(root) ≈ 0 is the real test.

column1: Evaluations to reach 1e-12 on [0, 1] for the diode equation?
column2: Bisection 41 (one bit per evaluation), brentq 14, newton from a good guess 7. Speed comes from using the function's shape; robustness from keeping a bracket.

column1: Operating point of 5 V, 1 kΩ and a diode (Is = 1e-14 A, VT = 25.852 mV)?
column2: Solve (5 − V)/1000 = Is(e^(V/VT) − 1) with brentq on [0, 1]: V = 0.6925 V, I = 4.3075 mA.

column1: What does curve_fit return?
column2: Best-fit parameters and their covariance matrix; standard errors are sqrt(diag(cov)). Needs a sensible starting guess p0 for nonlinear models.

column1: How do residuals reveal a wrong model?
column2: Random scatter at the noise level means adequate; long runs of one sign or a smooth curve mean missing physics (e.g. a one-exponential fit to two-exponential data: 49.7 mV RMS versus 8.5 mV).

column1: quad versus a rectangle sum?
column2: quad places points adaptively and returns an error estimate, handling infinite limits by a change of variables; fixed sums converge slowly for functions with kinks or infinite slopes such as sqrt(t).

column1: solve_ivp in one line?
column2: solve_ivp(f, (t0, t1), y0, rtol=…, atol=…, dense_output=True) integrates dy/dt = f(t, y); always set tolerances and compare with a known case (RC/RL exact solution).

column1: Why use SymPy in engineering?
column2: To derive or check algebra exactly (solve, simplify, diff, integrate), keep exact rationals (470000/53 Ω), and confirm two forms of a formula agree (simplify their ratio to 1 or difference to 0).

column1: Resistor that in parallel with 10 kΩ gives 4.7 kΩ?
column2: R2 = 470000/53 ≈ 8867.92 Ω; nearest standard parts 8.2 kΩ (4.505 kΩ) or 9.1 kΩ (4.764 kΩ).

column1: Interpolating a thermistor table: linear in R or in ln R?
column2: In ln R: the Beta model makes 1/T linear in ln R, so ln R interpolation is close to exact (37.46 °C vs exact 36.96 °C at 6 kΩ) while linear-in-R is 3.6 °C off; a spline in ln R is within 0.01 °C.

column1: Where does an RC low-pass cross −20 dB?
column2: At f = fc·sqrt(99) ≈ 9.95 fc, just below one decade above the corner, because the −20 dB/decade asymptote is approached gradually.

column1: Log or linear axes?
column2: Use log axes when data span decades (frequency response, leakage currents); dB on a log-frequency axis turns RC responses into straight-line asymptotes. Label every axis with quantity and unit.

column1: Why SVG/PDF for figures?
column2: Vector formats stay sharp at any size and keep text editable; PNG is a pixel grid (better only for very dense scatter plots or images).

column1: What is a notebook kernel, and why does it cause hidden state?
column2: The separate Python process that runs cells and keeps variables in memory in the order cells were RUN, not the order on the page; edited, deleted or out-of-order cells leave values the visible code doesn't explain.

column1: Before trusting or sharing a notebook?
column2: Restart the kernel and Run All (or execute it from a clean kernel with nbconvert/CI). Execution counts that don't read 1, 2, 3… from the top are the warning sign.

column1: Git working tree vs staging area vs commit?
column2: Working tree: files you edit. Staging area: changes selected with git add. Commit: permanent hashed snapshot of the staged project with author, date, message and parent.

column1: How does git name a file version?
column2: SHA-1 of 'blob <size>\0' + content (40 hex digits; 7-digit short form). Content-addressed: anyone can recompute and verify it; one changed character changes ~37.5 of 40 digits.

column1: Birthday bound for accidental hash collisions?
column2: P ≈ n²/(2N) for n objects and N possible hashes; 50% at n ≈ sqrt(2N ln 2). SHA-1 (N = 2^160): negligible by accident. 7-hex short hashes (2^28): 50% at ~19,000 commits.

column1: What makes a good unit test?
column2: An independent expected value: a hand-worked case, a symmetry, a bound, a conservation law, or an expected exception. Not the same formula as the code (it would share the bug).

column1: Default tolerances: math.isclose, pytest.approx, numpy.isclose?
column2: isclose: rel 1e-9, abs 0 (fails vs 0). approx: rel 1e-6, abs 1e-12. numpy.isclose: rtol 1e-5, atol 1e-8, asymmetric. Choose tolerances from the problem's scale.

column1: Testing a value whose correct answer is 0 (e.g. a KCL residual)?
column2: Relative tolerance of zero is zero, so use an absolute tolerance tied to the quantities involved: e.g. abs_tol = 1e-9 × the largest current at the node.

column1: assert or raise ValueError?
column2: raise for bad input from callers (can happen in correct code, must always be checked). assert for your own invariants and in tests; python -O deletes asserts.

column1: Why can't a statistical test with fresh seeds have tight limits in a big suite?
column2: False failures add up: 400 tests at ±3 SE fail somewhere 66% of runs. Fix seeds for repeatability, or widen limits (±4.21 SE for 1% suite-level false failures).

column1: Five practices for reproducible analysis?
column2: Script every step; record/pin the environment; seed randomness; keep raw data read-only and record its hash; re-run from a clean machine automatically (CI).

column1: What does git bisect do?
column2: Binary search through history for the first bad commit using a test script (exit 0 = good); at most ceil(log2 n) tests, e.g. 10 for 1000 commits. Works best with small, buildable commits.

column1: Why does this curriculum check numbers to half a unit in the last digit?
column2: A correctly rounded value lies within half a unit of the truth, so the check accepts exactly the correctly rounded values; it cannot detect errors smaller than the published precision.

column1: Diligence question that tests a team's engineering process?
column2: 'Pick a number in this report: how long to regenerate it from raw data?' Strong: minutes, a scripted target that CI reruns. Evasive: 'we'd have to find who ran it.'

column1: The four stages of a C build, and an error typical of each?
column2: Preprocessor (#include/#define; 'No such file'), compiler (syntax/types; 'expected ;'), assembler (object code), linker (joins objects; 'undefined reference' = declared but never defined/linked).

column1: Declaration vs definition in C?
column2: A declaration (prototype) gives name and types so code can call it; the definition has the body and exists in exactly one translation unit. Declarations go in headers.

column1: -7 / 2 and -7 % 2 in C vs Python?
column2: C truncates toward zero: -3 and -1. Python floors: -4 and 1. Both satisfy (a/b)*b + a%b = a. Wrap indices in C with ((i % n) + n) % n.

column1: Why is k / 4096 * 3300 zero for every 12-bit ADC code?
column2: Integer division happens first: k/4096 is 0 for k < 4096. Multiply first: k*3300/4096; add half the divisor to round: (k*3300 + 2048)/4096.

column1: Unsigned vs signed overflow in C?
column2: Unsigned arithmetic wraps modulo 2^n (defined). Signed overflow is undefined behavior; the optimizer may assume it never happens.

column1: Why is -1 < 1u false in C?
column2: Usual arithmetic conversions: mixing int and unsigned int converts the int to unsigned; -1 becomes 4,294,967,295. -Wextra (-Wsign-compare) warns.

column1: Integer promotion?
column2: Types narrower than int are converted to int before arithmetic: uint8_t 200 + 100 = int 300; stored back into uint8_t it becomes 44.

column1: Why does int64_t e = a * b; still overflow for int a, b?
column2: The product is computed in int, then widened. Cast an operand first: (int64_t)a * b.

column1: Size of long?
column2: Implementation-defined: 64 bits on Linux/macOS, 32 bits on Windows and 32-bit MCUs. Use <stdint.h> fixed-width types when width matters.

column1: Two meanings of static in C?
column2: File level: internal linkage (private to the translation unit). Inside a function: the variable persists for the whole program, initialized once.

column1: What does #define SQUARE(x) x*x give for SQUARE(1+2)?
column2: 5 (1 + 2*1 + 2): macros substitute text. Parenthesize ((x)*(x)) — still double-evaluates — or use a static inline function.

column1: Undefined vs implementation-defined behavior?
column2: Implementation-defined: chosen and documented per compiler (size of long). Undefined: no requirements at all (signed overflow, uninitialized reads, oversized shifts).

column1: Defense in depth against C undefined behavior?
column2: -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror; sanitizers (UBSan, ASan) in tests; static analysis; coding standards (MISRA C, CERT C); tests in CI.

column1: When does a uint32_t millisecond counter wrap, and how do you measure intervals across it?
column2: After 2^32 ms ≈ 49.7 days. Compute now - start in uint32_t (modular arithmetic gives the right answer for intervals under 49.7 days); never compare raw counts.

column1: &x, *p, p = q versus *p = *q?
column2: &x: address of x. *p: the object p points to. p = q re-points p; *p = *q copies the value. Assigning to p changes where it points, to *p what is stored there.

column1: How does a C function return several results?
column2: Return a status code (0 ok, negative error) and write results through pointer (output) parameters: int f(const T *in, size_t n, T *out1, T *out2).

column1: a[i] in terms of pointers, and pointer arithmetic scaling?
column2: a[i] is *(a + i). p + 1 advances by sizeof(*p) bytes: for int32_t*, p + 3 is 12 bytes on. Pointer differences count elements.

column1: Why must C functions take an array's length separately?
column2: Arrays decay to pointers when passed; sizeof the parameter is the pointer size (8 on 64-bit), not the array's. Pass n as size_t.

column1: Bytes needed for a C string of length L, and the safe way to build one?
column2: L + 1 (the zero terminator). Use snprintf(dst, size, ...): never overflows, always terminates, returns the needed length (>= size means truncated).

column1: Why is strcpy dangerous?
column2: It copies until the source's terminator with no idea how big the destination is; a long input overflows the buffer, a classic exploit path.

column1: Struct size of uint8, uint32, uint16 in that order vs largest-first?
column2: 12 bytes (3 + 2 bytes padding) vs 8 bytes. Fields align to their size; the total rounds to the largest alignment. Order fields largest first.

column1: Stack vs static vs heap storage?
column2: Stack: locals, freed on return, small. Static: globals/static locals, whole program, size known at link time. Heap: malloc/free, run-time size, must free exactly once.

column1: The realloc trap(s)?
column2: p = realloc(p, n) leaks the old block if realloc fails (returns NULL). And realloc may move the block: pointers into the old one dangle (use after free). Use a temporary; keep indices, not pointers.

column1: Why grow buffers by doubling?
column2: Copies form a geometric series ≤ final size: constant amortized cost per append. Fixed-step growth costs ~n²/(2·step) copies in total.

column1: The common memory bugs?
column2: Buffer overflow, use after free, double free, leak, dangling stack pointer, uninitialized read, null dereference. None is reported by C itself; ASan/LSan/UBSan catch most in testing.

column1: Why do safety-critical MCUs avoid malloc after start-up?
column2: Unpredictable allocation time, fragmentation in long-running devices, and no safe recovery from failure mid-loop. MISRA C forbids the standard allocators; use static or pool allocation.

column1: How big a share of serious vulnerabilities are memory-safety bugs?
column2: About 70% at Microsoft (CVEs 2006–2018) and Chromium (high-severity bugs); Android fell from 76% (2019) to under 20% (2025) as new code moved to memory-safe languages.

column1: Skeptical read of 'Rust has 1000x fewer memory-safety vulnerabilities'?
column2: Google's Android estimate rests on ~5 million lines and one potential vulnerability (n = 1). Direction credible; the exact ratio is a small-sample estimate. Ask about unsafe code and C boundaries.

column1: Value of an n-bit two's-complement pattern, and its range?
column2: S = −b(n−1)·2^(n−1) + Σ b(i)·2^i: the top bit has negative weight. Range −2^(n−1) to 2^(n−1) − 1 (8-bit: −128 to 127).

column1: Why is negation 'invert and add one'?
column2: x + ~x = 2^n − 1, so ~x + 1 = 2^n − x ≡ −x (mod 2^n). Exception: the most negative value negates to itself.

column1: Sign-extend a 12-bit field x portably?
Set, clear, toggle, test bit n?
column2: r |= 1u << n; r &= ~(1u << n); r ^= 1u << n; if (r & (1u << n)). Use unsigned types: 1 << 31 on a 32-bit int is undefined.

column1: Insert value v into a w-bit field at position p?
column2: r = (r & ~(mask << p)) | ((v & mask) << p) with mask = (1u << w) − 1. Clearing first matters: OR alone cannot lower bits.

column1: What does volatile do, and not do?
column2: Forces every read/write of the object to happen, in order (hardware registers, ISR-shared variables). It does not make read-modify-write atomic.

column1: The write-1-to-clear trap?
column2: Reading a W1C status register and writing back value | mask clears every pending flag you read, not just yours. Write only the bits you mean to clear.

column1: Little vs big endian for 0x0A0B0C0D?
column2: Little: 0D 0C 0B 0A at increasing addresses (x86, most Arm MCUs, RISC-V Linux). Big: 0A 0B 0C 0D (network byte order). Serialize with shifts, never by casting buffers.

column1: Q15: range, step, and the multiply?
column2: [−1, 1 − 2^−15], step 3.05e−5. (a·b + 2^14) >> 15 with a 32-bit product: rescale Q30 → Q15 with rounding; saturate (−1)·(−1).

column1: RMS error of rounding vs truncating to step Δ?
column2: Rounding: uniform ±Δ/2, RMS Δ/√12 (no bias). Truncation: uniform [−Δ, 0], RMS Δ/√3, mean −Δ/2 (biased). Each extra bit ≈ 6 dB.

column1: Why does a fixed-point EMA filter stop short of its input?
column2: The update α(x − y), truncated, becomes 0 once x − y < 1/α LSB: a dead band of ~1/α counts (half with rounding). Fix with more state bits or error feedback.

column1: Bit tricks: power of two, x mod 2^k, clear lowest set bit?
column2: (x & (x − 1)) == 0 for x > 0; x & (2^k − 1); x &= x − 1 (also the basis of a fast popcount).

column1: Why did the Patriot clock drift 0.34 s in 100 h?
column2: 0.1 chopped to 23 fractional bits is 0.1(1 − 2^−20); time = ticks × that constant, so the error grows with uptime. Keep time as integer ticks.

column1: How does the Internet (ones'-complement) checksum work?
column2: Sum 16-bit words, fold carries back in, complement. A receiver's sum including the checksum is 0xFFFF. Byte-order independent; misses swapped words.
